subject: chemistry
title: Electronegativity and bond polarity
key_idea: Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond. A difference in electronegativity makes a bond polar. A molecule is polar only if its polar bonds do not cancel because of the shape.

blocks.text: Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls on the bonding electrons. This section covers the factors and the trends.

items.meaning: The power of an atom to attract the pair of electrons in a covalent bond.
The scale of electronegativity values. Fluorine is the highest at 4.0.

items: A greater nuclear charge increases electronegativity.
A smaller atomic radius increases electronegativity, because the bonding pair is nearer the nucleus.
More shielding by inner shells decreases electronegativity.
Across a period, nuclear charge increases and the radius decreases with similar shielding, so electronegativity increases.
Down a group, the radius and shielding increase, so electronegativity decreases.
The most electronegative elements are at the top right of the Periodic Table, with fluorine highest.
Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element.

blocks.text: Ionic and covalent bonding are two ends of a continuum. This section covers how the electronegativity difference sets the type of bond.

items: Two identical atoms have no difference, so the pair is shared equally. This is a pure covalent bond.
A small difference gives an unequal share of the pair. This is a **polar covalent bond**.
A very large difference means one atom takes the electron completely. This is ionic bonding.
Between these extremes bonds have some ionic character and some covalent character.
In a polar bond the more electronegative atom has a partial negative charge, δ−.
The other atom has a partial positive charge, δ+.
For example in HCl, the H atom is δ+ and the Cl atom is δ−.
The separation of charge is a **permanent dipole**. Its size is the dipole moment.
The bigger the electronegativity difference, the more polar the bond.
A very large difference gives ionic bonding.
δ+ goes on the less electronegative atom.

blocks.text: A molecule with polar bonds may or may not be polar overall. This section covers how the shape decides.

items: Each polar bond has a dipole with a direction.
If the dipoles are arranged symmetrically they cancel, and the molecule has no overall dipole.
If they do not cancel, the molecule has an overall permanent dipole and is polar.
CO₂ is linear. Its two C=O dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, so it is non-polar.
H₂O is non-linear. Its two O–H dipoles do not cancel, so it is polar.
CCl₄ and BF₃ are symmetrical, so they are non-polar. NH₃ and CHCl₃ are not symmetrical, so they are polar.

items: Polar bonds do not always make a polar molecule.
Symmetrical molecules have dipoles that cancel.
Use the shape to decide.

checks.a: The power of an atom to attract the pair of electrons in a covalent bond.

checks.q: Explain why electronegativity decreases down group 17.
checks.a: The atomic radius and the shielding increase down the group. The bonding pair is further from the nucleus and less strongly attracted, even though the nuclear charge is greater.

checks.q: Explain why CO₂ has polar bonds but is a non-polar molecule, whereas H₂O is polar.
checks.a: The C=O bonds are polar because O is more electronegative than C. CO₂ is linear, so the dipoles cancel and there is no overall dipole. H₂O is non-linear, so the O–H dipoles do not cancel and there is an overall dipole.

items: Pauling electronegativity values are given in the question when they are needed.

Use the difference in values to predict whether a bond is ionic or covalent. As a rough guide, a difference of about 1.8 or more gives ionic bonding, a smaller difference gives polar covalent bonding, and no difference gives non-polar covalent bonding.
